findings.description: The inline policy grants wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) on Resource "*", violating least privilege. Compromise of this user's long-lived access key would permit full control of compute, storage, and serverless resources in the account, including data exfiltration from any S3 bucket, and privilege escalation via lambda:* (creating/updating functions that run under arbitrary passed roles) and ec2:* (instance profile attachment).

A permanent IAM access key is minted for a highly privileged user instead of using an IAM role with short-lived STS credentials. Because no pgp_key is supplied, the secret is written to Terraform state in cleartext, so anyone who can read the state file obtains non-expiring near-administrative credentials.

The svc_deploy_key_material output publishes access key material from the resource and is not marked sensitive = true, so it is rendered in plan/apply logs, CI output and root module outputs. Since no pgp_key is set, encrypted_secret is empty and the practical intent is to surface the secret, making this an unguarded credential disclosure path.

A programmatic IAM user is created with account-wide wildcard permissions and no permissions_boundary, so there is no upper bound constraining the effective privileges of the user or of any principal that escalates through it. Human-oriented MFA controls do not apply to an access-key-only user, but the absence of a boundary on a near-admin identity is a genuine access-control weakness.
